To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the integrated viral sequence of HBV in the HAGS 1.2.1 cell line is approximately 2.5 kb in length, and the cellular sequence is similar to a human satelite III sequence.
the integration sites of the HBV in the human hepatocarcinoma cell line, HBAG 2.1 were identified.
a combination of conventional PCR and IPCR is an effective method for the analysis of viral-cellular junction sequences in HAGS cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method for the identification of HBV DNA and flanking sequences, which may provide a better understanding of the mechanism of HBV integration into the human genome.
the molecular biology of HBV and the mechanism of HBV integration in the hepatoma cell line.
the analysis of the integrated HBsAg gene in the human hepatocellular carcinoma cell line, HAC 2.1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HBV DNA integration in the human hepatocellular carcinoma cell line, HAKS 2. 1, occurs by a nonhomologous recombination event and that the viral-cellular sequence is very similar to a satellite III sequence with GGAAT repeats.
the integration of HBV DNA into the cellular DNA in HAG 2.1 may have occurred through a nonhomologous recombination process, but the exact mechanism is still unclear.
HBV DNA is integrated in the genome of HAGS 22.1 cells and the integration sites of the viral DNA are within the X gene and the 5′ end of the C gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have cloned the HBV integrand in the HAGS 21 cell line and the junction between the integrated viral DNA and the host cell DNA has been identified.

the HBV integration site in HAGS cells is located at the 5'-flanking region of the human satellite III sequence, which is a highly repetitive sequence and is not a common integration site of the HBV genome.

the integration sites of HBV DNA in the liver cell line HAGS 1 and 2.1 are different, and the cellular sequence flanking HBV DNA in both cell lines is similar to a human DNA satellite III sequence with GGAAT repeats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of HBV DNA is not random but is associated with a specific cellular DNA sequence.
the combination of conventional PCR and IPCR can be used for the detection and analysis of integrated viral sequences.
the integration of HBV DNA into the host genome may play a role in the development of human hepatocellular carcinoma.
